title: CCAR-F (CCA-F) exam dumps: do they exist, and would they help?
description: CCAR-F (CCA-F) exam dumps: why the published exam design works against them, what the guide does not say, and what prepares a candidate instead.

faq.q: Are there real CCAR-F exam dumps?
faq.a: The CCAR-F exam guide requires every candidate to accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement before the exam begins, covering all questions, answer options and scenarios. Any genuine dump would therefore come from a breach of that agreement. This site does not assess or point to any source that claims to offer one.

faq.q: Can using an exam dump get me banned?
faq.a: Section 13 of the CCAR-F guide says cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content may result in invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential and a ban from future exams. It does not mention studying from leaked material. Anyone who shares exam content does put their own result and credential at risk.

faq.q: Would a dump help me pass CCAR-F?
faq.a: The guide describes 60 items built around 4 scenarios picked at random from a bank of 6, testing practical judgment about architecture, configuration and tradeoffs. A remembered answer set reflects someone else's draw and teaches answers rather than reasoning. Practice questions that explain why each option is right or wrong are a better use of limited time.

faq.q: What is the best free preparation for CCAR-F?
faq.a: Start with the official exam guide: Section 7 lists what to build, Section 8 gives hands-on exercises, and Section 9 has sample questions with explanations. Then a free ten-question diagnostic shows which domains need the most work.

body:
If you searched for CCAR-F dumps, here is the short answer. Everyone who has taken the Claude Certified Architect Foundations exam (CCAR-F, also written CCA-F) had to accept a confidentiality agreement before the first question appeared, promising not to disclose, reproduce or distribute any part of it. On our reading, that means a genuine dump could only exist because somebody broke that agreement. This article does not guess whether any real one exists, and it does not point to anywhere that claims to sell one.

The more useful answer is that even a genuine dump is a poor bet for this particular exam, for reasons that follow directly from how the published exam guide describes it. The rest of this article walks through those reasons, then covers what prepares you instead, most of it free. (If you are unsure which code is the official one, the guide's details table lists the exam code as CCAR-F.)

What a dump would have to contain

Section 3 of the CCAR-F guide sets out the shape of the exam: 60 items, a 120-minute time limit, and an exam structure described as "4 scenarios drawn from a bank of 6".

Section 5 explains what a scenario is: "Each scenario presents a realistic production context that frames a set of questions. During the exam, 4 scenarios are presented and picked at random from the full set of the 6 scenarios below."

Two things follow from that. First, you cannot know in advance which four scenarios you will get. A set of questions remembered from someone else's exam reflects the four they drew, not the four you will draw. Second, the questions are not free-standing facts. Each one sits inside a production context, and the context is part of the question.

Section 10 adds one more detail: "Scaled scoring models help equate scores across multiple exam forms that might have slightly different difficulty levels." So the guide says more than one form exists. It does not say how many, how they differ, or what changes between them, and this article will not fill that gap with a guess.

None of this makes the scenarios secret. You can read the six scenarios the guide publishes, and knowing them well is legitimate preparation. What nobody can tell you is which four you will face.

What the questions actually test

Section 1 of the guide is direct about the level: "Candidates must demonstrate not only conceptual knowledge but practical judgment about architecture, configuration, and tradeoffs in production deployments."

The format supports that. Section 3 lists the item format as "Multiple-choice and multiple-response items; each item states how many responses to select". In a multiple-response item, you pick that stated number of correct options from several plausible ones, which is where a remembered letter is least help. There is more on how each item states how many responses to select and what that means for how you read a question.

This is why the exam is hard in the way engineering judgment is hard. The right option depends on the constraints the scenario sets: what the system must guarantee, what it can afford, what has already failed. Change those constraints and a different option becomes correct. An answer key with no reasoning teaches you a letter for one set of constraints. It does not teach you to notice when the constraints have moved, and memorizing a rule can produce the wrong answer when they have.

The guide also shows you what real items look like. Section 9 says its sample questions "illustrate the format and difficulty level of the exam" and that they "are drawn from the practice test". So the guide's own samples come from a practice test, and the guide publishes them with explanations. Read those in the guide itself.

The agreement, and what the rules attach consequences to

Section 14 is short enough to quote in full:

Before the exam begins you must accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement. By accepting, you agree that all exam content, including questions, answer options, and scenarios, is the confidential and proprietary property of Anthropic, and that you will not disclose, reproduce, or distribute any portion of it. If you do not accept the agreement, the exam session ends and no refund is issued.

Section 13 sets the rules for the session itself. Among them, candidates must "Not capture, copy, photograph, or reproduce any exam content in any form". Its consequences clause reads:

Cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content may result in invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential, and a ban from future exams.

Section 15 adds that the obligation does not end at the exam room door: "Holders remain subject to the rules of conduct described in Section 13."

It is worth being precise about what these sections say. They attach consequences to cheating, to attempting to access prohibited resources, and to disclosing exam content. They say nothing about studying from leaked material, and this article does not claim they do. What they do make clear is that anyone who shares exam content is putting their own result and credential at risk to do it.

Twelve months, then a renewal

Section 15 opens: "The Claude Certified Architect – Foundations credential is valid for 12 months from the date it is awarded. Because the underlying technology evolves rapidly, the credential is time-limited so that holders maintain current knowledge."

Renewal is not a formality either. The guide says: "To renew on time, you review what has changed since you certified and complete a free, non-proctored assessment on the Anthropic Partner Academy." And: "If exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam to recertify rather than complete the renewal assessment."

The conclusion here is ours, not the guide's. The credential is built around keeping up with a technology that changes, and renewal means reviewing what has changed. Understanding can be updated. A list of remembered answers cannot: there is nothing in it to review, only something to replace.

What a failed attempt costs

If you were looking for a shortcut because time or money is tight, this is the part worth weighing.

Section 3 lists the exam fee as $125 USD, and Section 11 notes that the fee shown at checkout reflects any discount for your partner tier. Section 12 sets the retake policy: after a failed attempt you wait 14 days, then 30 days after a second, then 90 days after a third, and you may take the exam up to four times in a rolling twelve-month period. The same section is explicit that the fee applies to each attempt.

Two more rules can cost the fee without a result. Section 11 says changes made within 24 hours of your appointment forfeit it, and Section 12 says a no-show or late arrival forfeits it too.

The pass mark is 720 on a scale of 100 to 1,000, and it is a scaled score: Section 10 says the per-domain percentages on your score report are not used to decide a pass or fail. Walking in with answers that belong to a different draw of scenarios is a costly way to find out where you stand.

What works instead, free first

The guide itself is the best free starting point.

Section 7, "How to Prepare", lists concrete things to build: a complete agentic loop with the Claude Agent SDK, a real project configured in Claude Code, MCP tools with clearly differentiated descriptions and structured errors, a structured data extraction pipeline, and practice with prompt engineering, context management and escalation patterns. Section 8 turns several of these into step-by-step hands-on exercises. Section 9 gives you the sample questions with explanations. All three are in the guide, free, and written by the people who wrote the exam.

After that, test yourself against questions in the same format:

  • Start with a free ten-question diagnostic that needs no account. It scores you by domain, so you know where to spend your time.
  • Work through ten free questions with detailed explanations, and read the explanations for the options you got right as well as the ones you missed.
  • When you want the full range, there are 400 scenario-based practice questions, each with a written explanation, and a 60-question timed mock drawn at the guide's domain weights for the final days before your exam.

The point of any practice question is the reasoning behind it, not its letter. That is what carries over to the four scenarios you actually draw.

The short version

A genuine CCAR-F dump could only come from someone breaking the agreement every candidate accepts. Even then, it would reflect someone else's four scenarios out of six, it would teach answers rather than the judgment the exam is built to test, and it would age as the credential is designed to. The guide's own preparation list, exercises and sample questions are free, and practice that explains its reasoning is the preparation that transfers.
